provider: Oracle Cloud, Google Cloud, AWS, Microsoft Azure, Hetzner
tier: mixed: Always Free tiers on Oracle, Google Cloud and AWS; paid addresses on Azure and Hetzner

free_tier.stated: Oracle Always Free includes 1,500 OCPU-hours and 9,000 GB-hours a month plus 10 TB/month of egress, on a card that takes a USD 1.00 authorisation and reverses it. Google Cloud's free tier includes an e2-micro with 1 GB/month of egress. AWS includes 750 public-IPv4 hours a month. Azure and Hetzner record no free allowance: Azure's price cells all render as $- and Hetzner's /29 is sold at EUR 13.60/month plus EUR 34.90 setup.
free_tier.notes: Allowances combine compute time and bandwidth limits: Oracle and AWS provide hour-denominated allowances (OCPU-hours, GB-hours, 750 hours) alongside byte-denominated egress limits (10 TB monthly, 1 GB monthly). metered_on reflects compute hours as the headline quota, while byte allowances are documented separately.

per_object_cap.stated: not applicable: an address, not an object
per_object_cap.notes: The nearest equivalent is the smallest unit that can be allocated: a /29 prefix on Azure and Hetzner, one external IPv4 on Google Cloud, one public IPv4 on AWS. Hetzner's own figure of EUR 2.27 per usable IP against EUR 13.60 a month implies six usable addresses in the eight.

retention.stated: not applicable: an address, not an object. The nearest equivalent is the instance holding it: Oracle reclaims an Always Free compute instance that sits at 7-day p95 idle, and the address goes with the machine.
retention.notes: Activity-based, so days is null rather than 7: the clock is a rolling idle percentile, not a fixed lease. The facts record no reclaim rule for the other four providers; Oracle's is the only one with a clock, and it is the constraint the binding field names.

egress.terms: Metered, with a large free allowance on Oracle and a small one on Google Cloud: Oracle includes 10 TB/month on Always Free, Google Cloud's free e2-micro includes 1 GB/month, and AWS bills the address itself at USD 0.005/h with 750 free hours. Hetzner bills a /29 at EUR 13.60/month plus EUR 34.90 setup. Azure's address prices render as $- and are unverified.
egress.free_allowance: Oracle 10 TB/month on Always Free; Google Cloud free e2-micro 1 GB/month; AWS 750 public-IPv4 hours/month

interface_detail: Each provider exposes its own REST API and CLI for address objects, so rest is the nearest token in the closed set and cli is the other half. The schema's enum has no token for a cloud provider API and none for a subnet product. The address is a resource in the account: an external IPv4 on Google Cloud, a public IPv4 on AWS, a public IP prefix on Azure, a subnet on Hetzner, a public IP on an Oracle VNIC.
tooling: The provider's own REST API, SDK and CLI. No third-party wrapper exists or is needed, because the address is a resource in the account rather than a product with its own protocol. The work is a small driver that creates an instance, attaches the address, and recreates it when the provider takes the machine back. Access is not the problem here.
chaining: One of these sits behind the Workers AI gateway as the egress hop: the Worker calls the instance, the instance dials out from a cloud address, and because every one of the five is a single ASN the chain buys a second provider rather than a second network.

limits.value: 7-day p95 idle reclaim on Oracle Always Free: the machine is taken back and the address with it
Oracle Always Free includes 10 TB/month of egress, about 222 times 45 GB/month
Google Cloud free e2-micro includes 1 GB/month of egress, which 45 GB/month exceeds about 45 times over
AWS includes 750 public-IPv4 hours a month, which covers one address continuously (744 hours in a 31-day month) with 6 hours spare
Google Cloud external IPv4 costs USD 0.005/h while in use, USD 3.65/month, with no free allowance stated

limits_note: Three constraints fit none of the seven. Cost: Hetzner's /29 is EUR 13.60 a month plus EUR 34.90 setup, EUR 2.27 per usable IP, and AWS and Google Cloud charge USD 0.005/h per address, USD 3.65 a month. Unverified price: Azure offers a /29 public IP prefix but every price cell on its pricing page renders as hBc, so the price of that prefix is unverified rather than zero. Denominator: the five publish different address products, such as a prefix, a single address, or a subnet, so per-address cost is comparable while capacity is not.
binding_note: At 45 GB a month across about 599,000 requests nothing here is near a byte or request ceiling except Google Cloud's 1 GB/month free egress, and crossing that produces a bill rather than a stop; Oracle's 7-day p95 idle reclaim is the only constraint that removes the address, so it is the one that ends the arrangement.

identity_cost.detail: Oracle Always Free tier requires a credit card and executes a reversible USD 1.00 authorization. Registration requirements for other listed providers are unverified against recent signup flows.

reliability_note: All five are datacenter ranges registered to the cloud provider itself or to one of its own entities (ARIN DIRECT ALLOCATION for Oracle, Google Cloud and Azure; ARIN ALLOCATION for AWS; RIPE ASSIGNED PA for Hetzner), so an exit carries that cloud ASN's reputation, and on Oracle the address disappears with the reclaimed machine.
confidence_note: The ASN numbers and holders are measured with RIPE prefix-overview and the allocation class is measured for all five providers with one registry lookup each (ARIN for Oracle, Google Cloud, AWS and Azure; RIPE for Hetzner), on one address per provider. The free-tier and price fields are vendor-page reads, so the weakest rung the verdict depends on is documented, not measured.

notes:
Network positioning and ASN classification for major cloud providers used as exit sources. Prices and baseline quotas are documented under respective compute records.

Cloud virtual machines fail residential exit requirements because addresses reside in provider-owned datacenter allocations. RDAP lookup on 129.146.0.1 confirms DIRECT ALLOCATION under netname OPC1 (129.144.0.0 to 129.159.255.255). Additional addresses or larger prefixes within the same autonomous system do not provide network diversity. For example, a Hetzner /29 allocation provides eight addresses within a single ASN, and 19,416 IPv4 prefixes within AS16509 belong to a single registration entity. Cost does not present the primary obstacle: at 45 GB monthly volume, Oracle 10 TB monthly allowance and AWS 750 free hours cover bandwidth requirements, and Hetzner IP pricing is EUR 2.27 per usable IP. The constraint is the datacenter registration class rather than pricing.

Autonomous system announcement totals recorded on 2026-10-24: AS31898 (Oracle) announces 3,861 total prefixes and 2,852 IPv4 prefixes. AS396982 (Google Cloud) announces 3,924 total prefixes and 3,558 IPv4 prefixes. AS16509 (AWS) announces 25,440 total prefixes and 19,416 IPv4 prefixes. AS8075 (Azure) announces 1,355 total prefixes and 1,233 IPv4 prefixes. AS24940 (Hetzner Online GmbH) announces 96 total prefixes and 91 IPv4 prefixes. Each provider operates dedicated infrastructure under its own autonomous system.

Documentation details: Oracle free tier offers 1,500 OCPU-hours, 9,000 GB-hours, and 10 TB egress. AWS provides 750 monthly hours. Google Cloud documentation lists 0.005 per hour rates. Hetzner cloud pricing lists EUR 13.60 plus EUR 34.90 base pricing. Azure pricing cells render hBc with data-hide-meter-type-if-no-price='true', leaving the exact price unverified without account export.

Interface tokens are recorded as rest and cli, with address products documented in interface_detail.
